title: New Zealand regions
subtitle: Regions, seats and te reo names
reverseLabel: Regional council seat for which region
about: The sixteen regions of New Zealand, north to south, with the town where each regional council or unitary authority sits, followed by the established te reo Māori names for the regions and the three main islands.

cards.note: Whangārei is New Zealand's northernmost city and by far Northland's largest settlement, home to over a quarter of the region's people.
Auckland Council began on 1 November 2010, merging the regional council and seven city and district councils into one unitary authority.
Hamilton is named after Captain John Fane Charles Hamilton of HMS Esk, killed at the Battle of Gate Pā in 1864.
The name recalls Wairaka of the Mātaatua canoe, who cried that she would act as a man and paddled the drifting canoe ashore.
Gisborne District Council is a unitary authority; Cook first set foot in New Zealand here, at Tūranganui-a-Kiwa, in October 1769.
The 1931 Hawke's Bay earthquake killed 256 people and levelled much of Napier, which was rebuilt in the Art Deco style.
Stratford, rather than New Plymouth, was chosen as a compromise between the long-standing rival interests of north and south Taranaki.
The council trades as Horizons. North was added to the city's name in the 1870s to avoid confusion with Palmerston in Otago.
Parliament moved from Auckland to Wellington in 1865, partly because the more central site suited members travelling from the South Island.
Tasman District Council is a unitary authority; Richmond, its largest town, lies about 13 km south of Nelson near the head of Tasman Bay.
Nelson became a city by royal charter in 1858, making it the oldest city in the South Island; it is a unitary authority.
Blenheim is named after the 1704 Battle of Blenheim, won by the Duke of Marlborough, who also gave the region its name.
Greymouth takes its name from the Grey River, named in 1846 by the explorer Thomas Brunner after Governor George Grey.
The regional council trades as Environment Canterbury. Christchurch was named in 1848 after Christ Church, John Robert Godley's college at Oxford.
Dunedin, founded in 1848 by Free Church of Scotland settlers, takes its name from Dùn Èideann, the Scottish Gaelic name for Edinburgh.
The council trades as Environment Southland. Invercargill joins the Scots inver, a river mouth, to the name of Otago superintendent William Cargill.

cards.label: Te reo Māori name for
cards.note: The tail end of the land; it once meant the South Island south of the Waitaki River, but now usually refers to Southland.

cards.label: Te reo Māori name for
cards.note: The fish of Māui, hauled from the sea in tradition; it became an official name, alongside North Island, in 2013.

cards.label: Te reo Māori name for
cards.note: Usually translated as the waters of pounamu, or greenstone; it and the name South Island both became official in 2013.
